title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: "Then there's all the more reason to legalize your position, if you can," Dolly said.
"Yes, if I can," Anna said, suddenly in a completely different register — subdued, mournful.
"Surely a divorce isn't out of the question? I was told your husband had agreed to it."
"Dolly, I don't want to talk about that."
"All right, we won't," Darya Alexandrovna said quickly, noticing the look of pain that crossed Anna's face. "All I'm saying is that you take too dark a view of things."
"Me? Not at all! I'm always cheerful and happy. You see — _je fais des passions._ Veslovsky…"
"Honestly, I don't much like Veslovsky's tone," Darya Alexandrovna said, eager to change the subject.

"Oh, nonsense! He amuses Alexey, that's all — he's a boy, completely under my thumb. You know, I steer him wherever I want. Just as you'd handle your Grisha.… Dolly!" — she switched abruptly — "you say I take too dark a view of things. You can't understand. It's too awful! I try not to take any view of it at all."
"But I think you should. You ought to do whatever you can."

"What can I do? Nothing. You tell me to marry Alexey, and you say I don't think about it. I don't think about it!" she repeated, the color rising in her face. She got up, straightened her back, and let out a heavy sigh. With her light step she began pacing the room, stopping now and then. "I don't think of it? Not a day, not an hour goes by that I don't think of it, and blame myself for thinking of it — because thinking of it could drive me mad. Drive me mad!" she repeated. "When I think of it I can't sleep without morphine. But never mind. Let's talk calmly. They tell me — divorce. First of all, he won't give me one. He's under the influence of Countess Lidia Ivanovna now."
Darya Alexandrovna, sitting straight on her chair, turned her head, her face following Anna with sympathetic pain.
"You ought to make the attempt," she said softly.

"Suppose I make the attempt. What does it actually mean?" Anna said, plainly giving voice to a thought she had rehearsed a thousand times. "It means that I, hating him, but still admitting that I've wronged him — and I do consider him magnanimous — humiliate myself by writing to him.… All right, suppose I make the effort; I do it. Either I get a humiliating refusal or I get his consent.… Fine, say I have his consent.…" Anna was at the far end of the room now, and she stopped there, fiddling with the curtain at the window. "I have his consent. But my… my son? They won't give him to me. He'll grow up despising me, with his father — the man I abandoned. Do you understand? I love them equally, I think, but both of them more than myself — two creatures, Seryozha and Alexey."

She walked back to the middle of the room and stood facing Dolly, her arms pressed tightly across her chest. In her white dressing gown her figure looked grander and broader than usual. She bent her head and, with shining wet eyes, looked from under her brows at Dolly — a thin, pitiful little figure in a patched dressing jacket and nightcap, trembling all over with emotion.

"It's only those two creatures that I love, and one excludes the other. I can't have them together, and that's the only thing I want. And since I can't have it, nothing else matters to me. Nothing at all. It will end one way or another, and that's why I can't bear to talk about it. So don't blame me, don't judge me for any of it. You can't, with your pure heart, understand everything I'm going through." She went over, sat down beside Dolly, and, with a guilty look, glanced into her face and took her hand.

"What are you thinking? What are you thinking about me? Don't despise me. I don't deserve contempt. I'm simply unhappy. If anyone is unhappy, I am," she got out, and turning away, she burst into tears.

Left alone, Darya Alexandrovna said her prayers and went to bed. While Anna had been speaking she'd felt for her with all her heart, but now she couldn't make herself keep thinking about her. The memory of home and of her children rose in her imagination with a peculiar charm — quite new to her — a kind of fresh brilliance. That world of her own seemed so sweet and precious now that nothing could persuade her to spend one extra day outside it, and she made up her mind to head back the next day for certain.

Meanwhile Anna went back to her boudoir, picked up a wine-glass and let several drops of a medicine fall into it — the active ingredient being morphine. After drinking it off and sitting still for a little while, she went into her bedroom feeling soothed and in better spirits.

When she came in, Vronsky studied her closely. He was searching for traces of the conversation he knew she must have had with Dolly, having spent so long in her room. But in her expression — that contained excitement, that air of holding something in reserve — he could find nothing but the beauty that always cast its fresh spell on him, though he was used to it, the consciousness of that beauty, and the desire that it should work on him. He didn't want to ask what they had been talking about, but he hoped she'd offer him something of her own accord. All she said was:
"I'm so glad you like Dolly. You do, don't you?"
"Oh, I've known her a long time, you know. She's very good-hearted, I suppose, _mais excessivement terre-à-terre._ Still, I'm very glad to see her."
He took Anna's hand and looked questioningly into her eyes.

Misreading the look, she smiled at him. The next morning, despite her hosts' protests, Darya Alexandrovna got ready for the trip home. Levin's coachman, in his far-from-new coat and shabby hat, with his ill-matched horses and his carriage with the patched mudguards, drove with grim determination into the covered gravel forecourt.

Darya Alexandrovna disliked saying goodbye to Princess Varvara and the gentlemen of the party. After a day together, both she and her hosts were perfectly clear that they did not get on, and that it was better not to meet again. Only Anna was sad. She knew that with Dolly gone, no one would stir up in her again the feelings their conversation had stirred. It hurt to disturb those feelings, but she also knew it was the best part of her soul, and that this part of her would soon be smothered by the life she was leading.

Once they were out in the open country, Darya Alexandrovna felt a delicious sense of release, and she was tempted to ask the two men how they had liked being at Vronsky's, when suddenly the coachman, Philip, spoke up on his own:

"Rolling in money they may be, but three pots of oats is all we got. Cleaned out down to the last grain before the cocks crowed. What's three pots? A mouthful! And oats are down to forty-five kopecks now. At our place, no fear — anyone who comes can have all they can eat."
"The master's a tight one," added the counting-house clerk.
"Well, did you like their horses?" Dolly asked.

"The horses — no question about them. And the food was good. But it felt sort of dreary there to me, Darya Alexandrovna. I don't know what you thought," he said, turning his handsome, good-natured face to her.
"I thought the same. Well — shall we be home by evening?"
"We'd better be!"

Arriving home and finding everyone perfectly fine and especially charming, Darya Alexandrovna launched in with great animation, telling them about the trip out, how warmly she had been received, the luxury and good taste in which the Vronskys lived, their amusements — and she would not allow a word against them.

"You have to know Anna and Vronsky — I've got to know him better now — to see how lovely they are, and how touching," she said, speaking now with complete sincerity, forgetting the vague feeling of dissatisfaction and awkwardness she had felt while she was there.
